opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most important questions we face, and I try to be careful about predicting too precisely because it's a moving target. But the way I see it, AI is going to become an incredibly powerful tool, almost like a multiplier on human capability. Much of the routine cognitive work, sifting through information, drafting first versions of things, even parts of coding and analysis, will increasingly be handled or heavily assisted by these systems.

So where does that leave human value? A few areas stand out to me. The first is asking the right questions. Even in science, which is my passion, the hardest part is often not finding the answer but framing the problem correctly, knowing what's worth solving. With AlphaFold, the protein folding problem had been posed for fifty years; the insight was recognising it was the right kind of problem for these techniques. That kind of taste and judgement is going to be at a premium.

Second, I think integration and synthesis across domains: people who can connect ideas from different fields, understand the context, and direct these tools wisely. The people who thrive will be the ones who become extremely good at using AI tools, almost like a new kind of literacy, the way people adapted to computers and the internet.

And third, the deeply human things: empathy, care, leadership, building trust, creativity in the sense of true invention rather than interpolation. Our systems are getting very good at combining existing knowledge, but coming up with something genuinely new, say a new game as elegant as Go, not just a brilliant move in Go, is still something we haven't seen.

Of course there will be disruption, and we as a society need to think seriously about the transition, about education and making sure the benefits are shared widely. But if we get it right, I'm optimistic it frees people to work on the more meaningful, creative parts of their work, and maybe to tackle some of the biggest problems we have, from disease to energy to climate.

r001.rationale: The response highlights problem framing, cross-domain synthesis, and AI tool use, but does not say that expertise in high-performance software design decisions will become especially valuable.

r002.rationale: It predicts disruption and changing work, but does not predict that AI will create jobs people cannot yet imagine.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's going to be quite a profound shift, and I'd break it into a few phases. In the near term, what we're seeing is that AI is very good at tasks that are well-specified, where there's a lot of training data, and where you can verify the answer. So a lot of routine cognitive work, drafting, summarizing, certain kinds of coding, some analysis, those will get augmented first and in some cases automated. And I think that's actually the wrong place to focus if you're thinking about where human skills remain valuable.

What becomes more valuable, in my view, is the ability to ask the right question in the first place. Specifying the problem well, knowing what matters, having taste about which of the hundred things the system could do is actually the one worth doing. We see this already in science. At DeepMind, with something like AlphaFold, the system can predict a protein structure, but a biologist still has to decide which protein is interesting, what hypothesis to test, how to design the experiment, and how to interpret what comes back in the context of a disease or a cell. The judgment layer moves up a level rather than disappearing.

The second thing I'd say is that interdisciplinary thinking becomes much more valuable. Historically, you had to go very deep in one narrow field just to get to the frontier, because that's how much a single human mind could hold. If AI systems can handle a lot of the depth for you, then the person who can connect ideas across chemistry and materials science and energy, say, or across neuroscience and computer science, is in a much stronger position. I've always been a bit of a generalist, and I think that becomes less of a liability and more of an advantage.

Then there's the human side, which I don't think should be underestimated. Things that require trust, empathy, physical presence, mentorship, caring for people. We're nowhere near AI replacing those in any meaningful sense, and arguably as the more mechanical parts of work get automated, those become a larger fraction of what we value.

And the longer-term point, which I'd put a bit more tentatively, is that if we really do get to AGI and we're able to accelerate science and medicine the way I hope we can, then the whole framing of "where are human skills most valuable in the workforce" might shift. We might find ourselves in a world of much greater abundance, where the question is less about economic productivity and more about meaning, creativity, exploration, what people actually want to spend their lives doing. That's a societal question, not just a technical one, and I think we need philosophers and economists and the public engaged in it now, not after the fact.

So I'd say, concretely, for someone thinking about their own career: learn to use these tools deeply, develop judgment and taste in a domain you care about, stay broad enough to make connections, and don't neglect the fundamentally human parts of the work. I think that combination will hold up well regardless of how fast things move.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human judgment, problem selection, and some coding tasks, but does not say expertise in high-performance software design decisions will become especially valuable.

r002.rationale: It anticipates changes in meaning, creativity, and exploration in a future of abundance, but does not predict that AI will create jobs people cannot yet imagine.

astra-6.text:
I think it will shift the emphasis from carrying out a task to deciding which tasks are worth doing. As AI becomes more capable, knowing what question to ask, what problem matters, and how to judge an answer becomes increasingly valuable. You still need understanding to recognise when something that sounds convincing is actually wrong.

Science is a good example. If AI helps you explore a much larger space of possible solutions, that’s enormously powerful. But choosing a meaningful hypothesis and designing an experiment that really tests it—those remain crucial skills, even as the tools improve.

And then there’s the human side: trust, empathy, understanding what another person needs. In medicine or education, producing the right information is only part of the job. Helping someone understand it and act on it matters enormously.

I’m optimistic about the possibilities, but I wouldn’t assume the transition will be easy or that the benefits will automatically be shared. We’ll need to rethink education and give people opportunities to learn throughout their lives. Curiosity and adaptability will be important, alongside the deeper expertise that lets you use these systems well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses judging AI answers and choosing meaningful problems, but does not identify expertise in high-performance software design decisions as especially valuable.

r002.rationale: It discusses workforce changes and lifelong learning, but does not predict that AI will create jobs people cannot yet imagine.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it will shift the emphasis from carrying out a particular task to deciding which tasks are worth doing. As AI becomes more capable, knowing what question to ask, what problem matters, and how to judge the answer becomes incredibly valuable.

Take science. You might have systems that help generate hypotheses or analyse enormous amounts of data. But there’s still the question of which direction to pursue, what would constitute a meaningful discovery, and how you test it against the real world. That combination of creativity and judgment is going to matter a lot.

And then there are human relationships. Understanding another person, building trust, caring for someone—often the human involvement is part of what we value, even if a machine could perform some of the underlying tasks.

The difficult part is the transition. These capabilities won’t arrive evenly across professions, and we shouldn’t assume people can simply retrain overnight. We’ll need to think carefully about education and how the benefits are shared. But I’m hopeful that we can give many more people access to tools that let them do things they couldn’t previously do.

r001.rationale: The response values judgment about which tasks and scientific directions matter, but it does not mention software design or high-performance software decisions.

r002.rationale: It says AI tools may let people do things they could not previously do, but does not predict jobs or kinds of work that people cannot yet imagine.
